newsitem.title: USA: Ameritech creates on-line muni network.
newsitem.headline: Ameritech creates on-line muni network.

text.p: Chicago's Ameritech Corp is marketing a secure on-line network that lets public finance officials communicate with each other and create bond documents collaboratively via desktop computer, company officials said Friday.

"It's a first-of-its-kind service that automates the processes used by government and financial professionals to author bond documents. That is probably the key feature here," said Rob Lanesey, Ameritech's media relations manager.
"You're looking at a very document-intensive industry," he said.

To access the secure portion of the service, users dial into Ameritech's network and log on with a password. That enables them to draft and share documents, send faxes and e-mail, and set up audio conferences with other network members via desktop computer.

Code numbers are assigned to individual deals so that only those authorized to work on them can access the documents. The program alerts users if someone else is making changes to the same version of draft documents.
It also enables users to view rate information and read reports posted by other network members.
"It's a secure private network. It's not going out on the internet," Lanesey said.
The service does includes an internet web site where users can post releases for bondholders and the general public. But only the website postings can be accessed by the public.
The service works with any Windows desktop application.

"It's very easy to use," said Russ Comeau, first vice president at AMBAC Indemnity Corp, who uses it with WordPerfect and Excel programs. "Most of the professionals really are concerned more about their work and really don't want to learn sophisticated or complex technology."

Government subscribers pay a one-time fee of $99 for the software plus hourly charges, typically starting at bout $9 an hour, for network usage. Rates for private sector companies vary widely according to which services are contracted.
Comeau said the system speeds up the tedious process of revising draft documents and sending them by overnight mail to other participants in the deal.

"You can upload 100 pages in about five minutes. The other guy downloads it in five minutes. You've just saved two days and replaced it with 10 minutes," Comeau said. "All that traditional paper-moving would be replaced."

The service was officially introduced Feb 18 but has already been used for deals during its test phase. Arlington County, Va., used it to produce documents for a $26 million general obligation bond issue in October.
"This thing works," said John Petersen, president of Government Finance Group Inc and financial adviser for the deal.

"We had to make some adjustments before the preliminary offering statement and the final offering statement, and were able to do it in a matter of minutes as opposed to an overnight which would have delayed things a day," Petersen said.
He predicted the service or other electronic commerce services would become even more cost-efficient on the large, multi-party bond issues he calls "Cecil B. DeMille productions."

"On the big, complicated deals there can be some real advantages from simply the cost of transmitting documents back and forth. The more documents and the more parties to those documents, the greater the complexity and the cost of information flow," Petersen said.
Additionally, he said, scanning the documents with a keyword search can help locate specific information quickly.

So far Ameritech, the baby bell of the midwestern states, has signed 85 users on Public Finance.Com, including government and public agencies, financial advisers, underwriters, cash managers, public pension fund managers, rating agencies, corporate trustees, credit enhancers, financial printers and bond counsel, Lanesey said.
Within the next couple months, Ameritech hopes to add the NRMSRS to its network, allowing issuers to file 15c212 disclosure reports directly to them via the system, Lanesey said.

Petersen and Comeau predicted the paper-bound municipal securities world move increasingly to services such as Ameritech's, and eventually to the internet once internet security concerns are resolved.
"Within a short period of years, public finance is going to be dominated by eletronic commerce," Comeau said.
